title: Consistency Models
subtitle: Not one dial from weak to strong — a menu of promises about what a read can return
objectives: Define a consistency model as a contract about what reads may return
Distinguish strong, eventual, and the useful guarantees in between
Recognize which anomaly a user is actually complaining about
Choose the weakest model that keeps your product honest, and know what it costs

exercises.title: A consistency model is a contract about what a read may return — not a quality setting
exercises.body: Put data on more than one machine and the copies disagree for a while. Your read lands on one of them. A consistency model is the rulebook for that gap: it states exactly which values a read is *allowed* to come back with. *Strong* forbids nearly every surprise. *Eventual* forbids almost nothing. Both are contracts, not quality levels.
exercises.note: So "stronger" never means "more correct" — it means fewer legal surprises, bought with a coordination round trip on every operation, and paid for again during a partition by refusing to answer at all.

exercises.prompt: What is a consistency model, at bottom?
choices: A measure of how reliable a database is
A contract stating which values a read is allowed to return — and therefore which surprises are legal
A setting that makes data more accurate
The number of replicas you keep
exercises.why: A consistency model isn't a quality level, it's a specification: it enumerates what a read may legally return, which means it defines exactly which weird outcomes you've agreed to. Reading it as 'stronger is better' misses the point — the model tells you which bugs are impossible and which are your job to handle.

exercises.prompt: Strong consistency: a write completes, and a read immediately after returns the new value. What does that require?
choices: Coordination — someone must confirm the write is visible before the read can be answered, and that confirmation costs a round trip
exercises.why: To promise a read reflects the latest write, the system must know what the latest write IS — and with more than one machine that means asking, which costs a round trip you cannot optimize away. Strong consistency is therefore not a feature you enable; it's coordination you purchase, on every operation, at the price of the network's physics.

exercises.prompt: Eventual consistency guarantees what, exactly?
choices: If writes stop, all replicas will converge to the same value — with no promise about how long that takes or what you see meanwhile
Reads are correct within one second
exercises.why: Read the guarantee carefully: it says only that replicas agree in the end, given a pause in writes — it makes no claim at all about the interval you actually live in. That's why it's such a weak promise dressed in a reassuring word: 'eventually' is unbounded, and in a system that never stops writing, the precondition never arrives.

exercises.prompt: ______ consistency promises replicas converge if writes stop, but says nothing about what you read in the meantime.
exercises.why: It's a promise about the destination and not the journey — which is fine when the journey is milliseconds and alarming when it's a partition lasting an hour.

exercises.prompt: Why isn't 'just use strong consistency everywhere' the obvious answer?
choices: It's not supported by most databases
It costs a coordination round trip on every operation, and during a partition it means refusing to answer — you'd pay latency always and availability sometimes, for data that often doesn't need it
exercises.why: Strong consistency has a price on the happy path (unit 18's latency-vs-consistency) and a price on the bad path (refusing service during a partition), and both are charged whether the data needed the guarantee or not. Buying it for a like counter means every like waits on a quorum — you've paid for a promise nobody would have missed.

exercises.prompt: So what's the design question?
choices: How strong can we afford to be?
What's the weakest model that still keeps the product honest — because the weakest adequate model is the cheapest and most available one
Which model does our database support?
exercises.why: Every step toward stronger consistency buys you fewer legal surprises and costs latency and availability, so the goal is the least you can get away with rather than the most you can afford. 'Honest' is the bar: the model is adequate when no anomaly it permits would mislead a user into a decision they'd regret.

exercises.title: Between strong and eventual sits a menu of narrow promises, each forbidding one specific insult
exercises.body: Strong and eventual are only the two ends. The useful guarantees live between them and each bans exactly one anomaly. *Read-your-writes*: you always see your own writes. *Monotonic reads*: your view never moves backwards. *Causal consistency*: you never see an effect before its cause. Everything else stays legal — which is why they are cheap.
exercises.note: Users never ask for these by name. They say "my comment vanished", "the count went down", "there's a reply to a message I can't see" — three complaints, three different missing promises.

exercises.prompt: A user posts a comment, then refreshes — and their own comment is gone. Which guarantee were they expecting?
choices: Read-your-writes: you always see your own writes, even if others see them later
exercises.why: They don't need to see everyone's comments instantly — they need to see THEIR OWN, because they know they wrote it and its absence looks like data loss. Read-your-writes is exactly that narrow promise, and it's much cheaper than strong consistency: route that user's reads to a replica that has their write, and everyone else can lag freely.

exercises.prompt: Match each guarantee to the anomaly it forbids.

pairs.right: Your own write vanishing after you make it
Time appearing to run backwards on refresh
Seeing an answer before the question
Every anomaly above, at coordination cost

exercises.why: Each middle guarantee names one specific way reality can look broken and forbids just that one — which is why they're useful. You buy the narrow promise your product actually needs instead of the total order you can't afford, and you get most of the felt correctness for a fraction of the cost.

exercises.prompt: Two refreshes: the first shows a new message, the second doesn't. Which guarantee is missing?
choices: Monotonic reads — successive reads should never move backwards in time for one user
exercises.why: Two reads landed on replicas with different lag, so the second answered from an older state — the data was never corrupt, the user just time-travelled. Monotonic reads forbids that specific insult, and the usual mechanism is routing each user's reads to a consistent replica so their view only ever advances (with the caveat from unit 10 that re-pinning can break it).

exercises.prompt: A chat shows a reply before the message it replies to. Which guarantee is missing?
choices: Consistent prefix / causal consistency — writes that caused each other must appear in that order
exercises.why: Nobody needs a global order of every message in the world — they need effects to follow their causes, because a reply arriving before its question isn't stale, it's nonsense. Causal consistency preserves exactly the ordering that carries meaning and leaves genuinely unrelated writes free to arrive in any order, which is why it's often the sweet spot for anything conversational.

exercises.prompt: Why is causal consistency so much cheaper than strong consistency?
choices: It only orders writes that are actually related, leaving unrelated writes to be applied in any order — so most operations need no global agreement
exercises.why: Strong consistency insists every write take a place in one global sequence, which means everyone agreeing about everything, all the time. Causal only insists that a write which depended on another comes after it — and in a system with millions of unrelated users, almost nothing is causally related, so almost nothing needs coordinating.

exercises.prompt: Your product needs users to see their own edits instantly, but is fine if other users see them a second later. What should you buy?
choices: Read-your-writes for the author, eventual for everyone else — that's the actual requirement, precisely stated
exercises.why: Stating the requirement exactly reveals how narrow it is: one person needs to see one thing immediately, and the entire rest of the world can lag. Strong consistency would satisfy that requirement and charge everyone a quorum for it. Most 'we need strong consistency' claims dissolve like this once someone writes down who actually needs to see what, and when.

exercises.title: Users report symptoms, and the clue that names the bug is usually *whose* read it was
exercises.body: Nobody files a ticket saying "read-your-writes is missing". They say: "the like count went *down*." The shape of the complaint is the diagnosis. The write landed and spread, so nothing is broken except which replica *their own* read hit. Read every complaint for who saw what, and when.
exercises.note: Rule out latency first. Stale is wrong-but-fast; slow is right-but-late. In a ticket they read identically — "the site is bad" — and they need opposite fixes.

exercises.prompt: A user says 'I changed my profile photo and it still shows the old one, but my friend can see the new one.' Diagnosis?
choices: Read-your-writes is missing for this user — their read is hitting a replica that lags behind their own write
exercises.why: The detail that identifies it is that the friend CAN see it — the write clearly succeeded and propagated, so nothing is broken except which replica the author's own read landed on. Notice the bug is defined by whose read it is rather than by the data, which is exactly why the fix is routing rather than a stronger database.

exercises.prompt: A user deletes a photo, gets confirmation, and it reappears in their feed ten minutes later. What likely happened?
choices: The delete and a stale cached copy raced — or a replica that never learned about the delete served it back
The photo was restored from backup
exercises.why: The resurrection of deleted data is a classic and it's usually a copy that never heard the news — a cache entry, a lagging replica, or a search index that indexed before the delete and was never told. Deletes are the nastiest case for derived copies because absence propagates badly: a copy holding stale data looks identical to a copy holding data that's supposed to exist.

exercises.prompt: A user reports 'the site shows me old data sometimes.' Which could cause it? Select all.
choices: Replication lag on a read replica
A CDN or browser cache serving a stale copy
A search index that hasn't been updated yet
exercises.why: Every copy is a chance to be behind — replicas, caches, and derived indexes are all the same shape of problem wearing different names, which is why 'stale data' incidents so often involve hunting the layer responsible. A slow query is different: it returns the RIGHT answer, late. Stale means wrong-but-fast; slow means right-but-late, and they need opposite fixes.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'eventually consistent' a bad answer to give a user or a product manager?
choices: Because it names the mechanism, not the promise — the honest version states a bound: 'usually under a second, and here's what you'll see meanwhile'
exercises.why: 'Eventually' describes what the database guarantees and answers nothing anyone actually asked — how long, and what does it look like in the gap? Users and product owners can reason about 'up to two seconds, and you always see your own changes immediately'. Turning the mechanism into a stated bound with an observable behaviour is what makes the tradeoff decidable rather than mystical.

exercises.prompt: Your team says 'we need strong consistency.' What's the first question to ask?
choices: Which read, by whom, must reflect which write — and what would actually go wrong if it were two seconds late?
How many replicas do we need?
exercises.why: 'We need strong consistency' is almost always a feeling standing in for a specific fear, and naming the fear usually shrinks it — often to read-your-writes for one user on one screen. And if the honest answer to 'what goes wrong?' is a real, irreversible loss, then you've justified the coordination cost with evidence instead of anxiety.

exercises.prompt: Which of these complaints is NOT a consistency problem?
choices: 'The like count went down when I refreshed'
'I see a reply to a message I can't see'
exercises.why: A slow page is a latency problem — the answer would have been correct, it just took too long, which is unit 4's territory and needs completely different tools. The other three are all correct-data-arriving-in-a-surprising-order: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and causal consistency respectively. Diagnosing which family you're in is the whole first move.

exercises.title: `W + R > N` buys you overlap, and overlap is not strong consistency
exercises.body: A key lives on `N` replicas. A write waits for `W` of them to acknowledge it; a read asks `R` of them. If `W + R > N` the two sets *cannot* be disjoint — pigeonhole — so at least one replica you read holds the newest completed write. That is the entire guarantee: a fresh copy is somewhere in your read set.
exercises.note: It does not tell you which of the returned values is newest, does not resolve a write still in flight, and is not linearizability. That needs a leader or consensus — unit 20. Arithmetic alone won't buy it.

exercises.prompt: Quorum reads and writes: N=3 replicas, W=2, R=2. What does W + R > N actually guarantee?
choices: That every read returns the latest value, always
Overlap: the read set and the write set must share at least one replica, so at least one node you read has seen the newest completed write
Nothing — the arithmetic is a coincidence
That writes are applied in order
exercises.why: It's pigeonhole arithmetic: write to 2 of 3 and read from 2 of 3, and the sets cannot be disjoint, so at least one replica you asked holds the newest completed write. Read that guarantee narrowly, though — overlap is necessary for a fresh read and NOT sufficient for strong consistency. A read racing an in-flight write can legitimately come back with either value; concurrent writes still have to be merged by some rule; and a 'sloppy' quorum that accepts writes onto substitute nodes can overlap with a set that never held the write at all. Real linearizability needs coordination — a leader, or consensus — which is what unit 20 is about. Arithmetic alone doesn't buy it.

exercises.prompt: Same 3 replicas, but W=1 and R=1. What did you buy and lose?
choices: Fast writes and fast reads that stay available if replicas are down — and no overlap guarantee, so a read can easily miss the newest write
exercises.why: W+R = 2, which isn't greater than 3, so the sets can miss each other entirely and you're squarely in eventual consistency. What you got in exchange is real: one replica is enough to serve, so writes and reads are fast and survive two nodes being down. That dial is the CAP tradeoff exposed as a config knob, and it's per-query in some systems — strict for a payment, loose for a feed.

exercises.prompt: You're designing 'items remaining in stock' shown during checkout for a limited product drop. Slide toward your model.
exercises.why: Overselling a limited drop is a real-world commitment you cannot take back — you take money for something that doesn't exist and then apologize to strangers. Coordination on the decrement is worth the latency here, precisely because the wrong answer creates an obligation. Contrast the same number on a browsing page, where stale stock costs nothing: the data is identical and the cost of being wrong is not.

exercises.prompt: Someone proposes 'use timestamps — the newest write wins.' What's the flaw?
choices: Different machines' clocks disagree, so 'newest' depends on whose clock you believe — and a skewed clock can silently discard a genuinely later write
exercises.why: Last-write-wins quietly assumes a shared global clock, and there isn't one — clocks drift, get corrected, and disagree by more than the interval between two writes. A machine running slightly fast can stamp a write far in the future and win every conflict for hours. This is why serious systems use logical clocks or version vectors, which order events by causality instead of trusting a wall clock nobody agrees on.

exercises.prompt: Can one product use several consistency models at once?
choices: Yes, and it should: payments strong, profile edits read-your-writes, feeds eventual — each dataset gets the weakest model that keeps it honest
exercises.why: Consistency is a property of an operation on a piece of data, not a badge worn by a company — so forcing one model everywhere means either overpaying for your feed or under-protecting your money. Mixing deliberately is the mature position, and the work is knowing which data is which, which is a product question rather than a database one.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of consistency models?
choices: Stronger is better; use the strongest you can afford
They're contracts about what a read may return: stronger forbids more surprises and costs coordination, so pick the weakest model that keeps the product honest — per dataset, not per company
exercises.why: Every model is a deal — fewer legal surprises in exchange for latency and availability — and 'strongest affordable' is the wrong instinct because it pays for guarantees nobody would have missed. This is the same question the course has asked since unit 5, now with formal names: you have copies, copies can disagree, and the model is you deciding exactly how much disagreement is allowed to reach a user.
